News and gap analysis

Two InfraNodus text networks built from our own material, plus a live analysis of the actual headlines.
  1. News and semantic graph. 322 Alpaca headlines published in the 3 days before each short we took since 29 Apr 2026, each tagged with what the trade did: faded, small loss or continuation loser. The tags are nodes, so you can see which words sit next to the losers.
  2. Strategy gap graph. 46 statements from the Nov 24 call, Chris's Nov 14 brief, the email thread, our results and the idea board. Gaps between clusters are where new tests come from.
Each graph is embedded full size below. Click a node to see its statements; the graph's own AI panel answers questions about it.

data.text/html:
How InfraNodus works

InfraNodus turns text into a network of concepts and then reads the shape of that network.
  1. Words become nodes. Each statement is cleaned (stop words removed, words lemmatised), and every remaining word is a node. Our outcome tags (faded, small loss, continuation loser) are added as nodes too.
  2. Co-occurrence becomes edges. Two words that appear close together in a statement are linked; the more often, the heavier the link. "price ↔ target" is the heaviest edge in the news graph because analysts publish so many target changes.
  3. Betweenness centrality finds the hinges. A word that sits on many shortest paths between other words connects topics. In the news graph price, result and report are the hinges; in the gap graph it is percent, minute and open.
  4. Community detection finds the topics. Groups of words that link to each other more than to the rest form clusters (Louvain modularity). The news graph splits into AI/data-center deals, analyst price targets, earnings results and insider selling.
  5. Structural gaps are the ideas. Two big clusters with few links between them are topics people discuss separately but never connect. Bridging a gap means asking how the two relate, and that question is usually a new hypothesis. Example: earnings results and analyst price targets sit in separate clusters, yet both precede our shorts; does a results headline that is followed by target raises behave differently?
Why this helps a trading group. It is a disciplined way to brainstorm: instead of asking "what else could work?", it points at the specific pair of topics we have not connected yet. Every gap it finds still gets tested on the data before it counts.

6. What this suggests testing

  • Earnings and guidance headlines carry the highest continuation-loser rates in this window, which matches Chris's finding that strong positive earnings shocks are the dangerous subset. Candidate veto: skip shorts with a same-day results or guidance headline, then check it on the tune year and the holdout separately.
  • Analyst target headlines look no different from the baseline here, despite what the graph's answer suggests. That is why every graph answer gets checked against the table above.
  • No-news spikes are the cleanest test of the short-covering thesis. Their row shows how they behave so far.
  • Only seven months of news (Alpaca's archive for these names starts around Apr 2026), so treat every rate here as a lead, not a rule. Massive or EDGAR history would extend it.
